articles.full_text:
EU Greenwashing Rules Push Lufthansa to Swap Green Fare Name for Impact Fare
- New fare name: Lufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fare, launched in 2023, to Impact Fare.
- Regulatory driver: The company cited new rules on environmental communication without naming the regulation.
- SAF funding: Each booking funds extra SAF equal to 10-20% of a flight’s estimated emissions.
Lufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fare to Impact Fare. The fare lets passengers fund emissions reduction and removal, and more than 5 million have booked it since 2023. The company cited “new regulatory requirements for environmental communication” as the driver for the change.
For every Impact Fare booking, Lufthansa Group deploys extra Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), a lower-emission jet fuel. It does so within six months of departure. On flights within Europe, the SAF volume is based on 20% of the flight’s estimated CO2 emissions. The remaining 80% sets a contribution to climate projects that avoid or remove CO2 outside the company’s value chain.
On intercontinental routes, the ratio is 10% to 90%. Customers can book the fare in all travel classes, and they receive extra Miles and Points. The group did not disclose the fare’s price or when the new name takes effect. “The new name places even stronger emphasis on customers’ contribution to greater sustainability in aviation,” the company said.
Regulatory Backdrop
The rename closely follows the start of application of the EU’s Directive on Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition (ECGT). The directive targets misleading green claims and other greenwashing practices. It also bans unverified generic claims such as “environmentally friendly” or “biodegradable.”
Last year, Lufthansa and other airlines agreed with the European Commission to stop using claims that national consumer authorities saw as misleading. These included claims that paying extra fees for climate projects or SAF could offset flight emissions. The deal followed a complaint by the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), a consumer advocacy group. BEUC also asked authorities to make airlines refund green fees paid on the basis of misleading claims.

Why It Matters
The fare is one of Lufthansa Group’s five approaches to lower-emission aviation, alongside fleet renewal, fuel efficiency, SAF use and intermodality. It serves private and corporate customers who want to fund extra sustainability measures. If the new name satisfies the tighter claims rules, Lufthansa could keep selling passenger-funded SAF to corporate travel buyers.

articles.title: European Commission Proposes Climate Resilience Law Built on a 3°C-by-2100 Warming Baseline
articles.summary:
The European Commission has presented an EU Framework for Climate Resilience to help Europe anticipate and manage climate risks. Its core is a proposed Climate Resilience Law that would give […]
The post European Commission Proposes Climate Resilience Law Built on a 3°C-by-2100 Warming Baseline appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
European Commission Proposes Climate Resilience Law Built on a 3°C-by-2100 Warming Baseline
- Shared warming baseline: The proposed law gives Member States a common trajectory reaching 3°C by 2100.
- €70 billion a year: Adapting Europe’s infrastructure and economy is expected to need about €70 billion annually.
- New online tools: A European resilience platform will host a hazard map, a tool navigator and a solutions showcase.
The European Commission has presented an EU Framework for Climate Resilience to help Europe anticipate and manage climate risks. Its core is a proposed Climate Resilience Law that would give Member States a shared warming trajectory for risk assessments. The Commission said it will begin implementing the Framework immediately.
Under the proposal, Member States would plan against warming of 1.5°C by 2030, 2°C by 2050 and 3°C by 2100. The Commission said current scientific evidence puts the world on that path. The Framework also aims to embed resilience across all major domestic and international policy areas. However, the Commission did not disclose when the law would take effect or how it would be enforced.
The Commission linked the Framework to this summer’s heatwaves and droughts. These drove some of Europe’s biggest rivers to historically low levels. It estimates climate damages cost about €200 billion from 2022 to 2025, or €50 billion a year. “Europe is warming at double the global rate. To become truly climate resilient, we need to adjust and learn along the way. Today, we are presenting a European approach to climate risks – to anticipate, to prepare for and to manage. We are ensuring that climate resilience will be included in policies across the continent, supporting investment, innovation and long-term growth,” said Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission.
Platform Tools and Next Steps
The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) developed a European Climate Viewer that maps projected hazards. It will later add supercomputing through the Commission’s Destination Earth initiative. Meanwhile, the European Environment Agency (EEA) built a Navigator that matches tools to a user’s location, sector and risks. A Solutions Explorer will also showcase measures tested through the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.
Separately, the Commission is developing a European Heatwave Plan, a Climate Insurance Alliance and a European Water initiative. It will also identify Europe’s 100 most climate-vulnerable territories and launch a PreparEU Advisory Group. An EU strategic plan on climate resilience will follow in 2028.
RELATED ARTICLE: European Commission to Withdraw Greenwashing Regulation
Who It Affects
- Member States: One national strategic plan would replace existing planning obligations, alongside more regular climate risk assessments.
- Local and regional authorities: The Framework offers pilot projects and advisory services to help them adapt.
- Businesses: The Commission wants them to scale up a European resilience industry. It projects the global adaptation market will reach €3.5 trillion by 2050.

articles.title: Position Paper: Priorities for the SFDR 2.0 trilogue negotiations - Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)
articles.summary: Position Paper: Priorities for the SFDR 2.0 trilogue negotiations  Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

source_detail.name: Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

articles.full_text:
With trilogue negotiations on the review of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) now under way, IIGCC has published a position paper setting out investor priorities for a revised framework that is both credible and usable in practice. 
 The paper welcomes the progress made by the European Parliament and Council. Both have kept a dedicated product categorisation system, including a Transition category that recognises the critical role of investment strategies that finance real-economy decarbonisation. However, important gaps remain. If they are not addressed, they could undermine the integrity and coherence of the rulebook, and investors’ ability to implement it. 
IIGCC calls on the co-legislators to:
- Ensure the Transition category is fit for purpose, safeguarding its integrity while facilitating transition finance, by anchoring eligibility in credible, time-bound and measurable transition plans.
- Maintain the Parliament’s safeguards on any opt-out for alternative investment funds available only to professional investors, including a prohibition on sustainability-related fund names.
- Retain product-level engagement disclosures across all three categories on a comply-or-explain basis, focused on how firms apply their entity-level engagement strategies.
- Preserve a limited baseline of decision-useful principal adverse impact indicators, particularly core climate indicators for Transition products, complemented by indicators tailored to each product’s strategy.
- Uphold the inclusion of general-purpose sovereign debt in the Transition category, and extend this to non-EU sovereign debt that meets credible climate criteria.
- Ensure the framework works across all asset classes through tailored Level 2 criteria, and apply the revised Regulation and related changes from a single date.

articles.title: USGBC Presses Data Center Owners on Transparency, Renewable Power and Waste Heat Reuse
articles.summary:
The U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) is working with data center teams and owners to highlight sustainability in development and operations. Its leaders outlined the work Tuesday at the 2026 […]
The post USGBC Presses Data Center Owners on Transparency, Renewable Power and Waste Heat Reuse appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
USGBC Presses Data Center Owners on Transparency, Renewable Power and Waste Heat Reuse
- Transparency push: USGBC says weak sustainability transparency has hurt some data center owners’ community engagement.
- LEED footprint: More than 2,000 data centers globally are LEED-certified and registered, covering 591 million square feet.
- Community deals: USGBC sees home retrofit payments and battery storage as possible terms in local data center agreements.
The U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) is working with data center teams and owners to highlight sustainability in development and operations. Its leaders outlined the work Tuesday at the 2026 Greenbuild International Conference + Expo, where data centers were a focus. “Data center owners and developers are recognizing that they need to be more transparent” about sustainability, said Elizabeth Beardsley, senior policy counsel at USGBC. “The lack of transparency, in some cases, has hindered their community engagement and backfired in terms of public sentiment,” she said.
More than 2,000 data centers globally were LEED-certified and registered as of September, according to USGBC. They represent 591 million square feet of space. LEED, short for Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design, is a widely recognized green building certification standard. About 350 U.S. data centers are LEED-certified, according to Beardsley.
USGBC is also working on several compliance pathways for data center building performance, Beardsley said. Earlier this year, USGBC and partner organizations launched the Greening AI Data Centers Coalition to set global sector standards. Meanwhile, four states have data center-specific building performance disclosures, and others have benchmarking laws requiring energy-use reporting. Beardsley did not name the four states or give a timeline for the new compliance pathways.
Beardsley called the growing dialog among stakeholders and communities about these facilities a positive development. Some communities gain significant money from data centers, she said, which could lower taxes, fund local energy resources and boost resilience. Possible agreements include payments for residents’ home efficiency retrofits, or battery storage that cuts peak energy use and adds resilience for local homeowners. “There are different models that are cropping up that I think have a lot of potential, but all those require a lot of coordination from all the different parties — the data center owner and developer, the utility, the community and the jurisdictions,” she said.
Renewable energy is another potential sustainability feature of these facilities, Beardsley said. Polls show residents are more likely to accept data centers powered by renewable or clean energy, she added. “We’re incentivizing use of renewable energy, and I think we see opportunity … to do even more in terms of encouraging some of those community energy best practices and opportunities, like reuse of waste heat,” she said.

Why It Matters
For USGBC, the compliance pathways and coalition seat add a standard-setting role on top of LEED’s existing data center base. That could make LEED a ready compliance route for owners under state disclosure or benchmarking laws, if the pathways match those rules.

articles.title: Nature recovery plan launched amid Northern Ireland biodiversity decline - Belfast Telegraph
articles.summary: Nature recovery plan launched amid Northern Ireland biodiversity decline  Belfast Telegraph
articles.full_text:
A new nature recovery strategy has been launched for Northern Ireland amidst warnings the region is the “most nature-depleted part of the UK”.
Agriculture minister Andrew Muir said he has heard calls from the public “time and time again” to “invest in nature and biodiversity”.
In Northern Ireland 36% of all features within protected areas are in unfavourable condition, and 12% of species assessed on the island of Ireland are threatened with extinction, according to the State of Nature Report for NI.
Stormont’s Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) says the new Nature Recovery Strategy for Northern Ireland to 2032 provides a framework for collective action, guided by science and evidence.
It identifies a number of pressures and threats for Northern Ireland’s environment including invasive species, climate change, inappropriate development, land and sea use change, increased intensive farming practices, and pollution.
The plan supports the wider international effort to reverse biodiversity loss, including the 30 By 30 ambition to effectively conserve and manage 30% of terrestrial and inland water areas, and 30% of marine and coastal areas, for nature and biodiversity by 2030.
The strategy also aims to restore degraded habitats including peatlands, wetlands, rivers, native woodlands and species-rich grasslands.
It further includes a “sustainable agricultural programme” outlining an aim to “implement policies and strategies that benefit our climate and environment while supporting our economically and socially significant agri-food sector”.
Heather McLachlan, National Trust director for Northern Ireland, said they have “been waiting for a number of years” for the statutory strategy.
Speaking at the Black Mountain in Belfast she said: “There’s a piece here about how do you then change that policy and that legislation into delivery on the ground.
“So here at Divis you’re seeing exactly that happening.
“So we have been working here for around 15 years, we are looking at not only where you look at species recovery, but also habitat.
“So Divis is well known for its peatland habitat, which is great for storing water and also for carbon, so in terms of climate change, it’s really really important.
“And in terms of these big weather events that we’re seeing at the moment, they are holding back water from the likes of Belfast City, so it has a big role to play not only for nature but also for the people of the city.”
She added: “I would have to say that in Northern Ireland, we’re the most nature-depleted part of the UK and possibly Europe as well, so we’ve got a real challenge here.
“We really haven’t been investing in nature for a number of years, and we probably need to change that because if you think about where we get our food from, where we get our water from, where we get our air from, all things that we all need individually, if we don’t look after that, it comes from nature.
“And therefore the big weather events that we’re seeing, some of the things that nature does is actually protects us from some of the big issues that come along and can help us manage them.
“So we, for the future, need to be very much investing in nature to make sure we’ve got soils which are allowing us to grow our food and also clean the water that we drink every day.”
Mr Muir said restoring nature “isn’t just a nice to have; it’s absolutely essential”.
“This is an important day where we put in place the building blocks for nature recovery and absolutely central to that is environmental organisation,” he said.
“They’re doing good work, including here at Divis, and they’ll be critical for the delivery of the actions that arise from this strategy.”
Asked about financing the plan given the financial pressures facing all Stormont departments, the minister said “investing in nature delivers massive benefits”.
“It delivers better water quality, better air quality, reduces our greenhouse gas emissions, but also connects communities together and you’re seeing this happen here at Divis,” he said.
“There are three key issues for this strategy going forward.
“Yes, it’s funding, and we’re already delivering significant investment, whether it’s from my department, through Shared Ireland, and Peace Plus, but also it’s in relation to people on the ground to do the job and the political support.
“The public keep telling us time and time again: invest in nature and biodiversity, and it’s important we fulfil their desires for the future.”

articles.title: Iberdrola Returns to U.S. Debt Market with $1.6 Billion Green Bond Issuance - ESG Today
articles.summary: Iberdrola Returns to U.S. Debt Market with $1.6 Billion Green Bond Issuance  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
Spanish multinational energy company Iberdrola announced that it has raised $1.6 billion in a green bond issuance in the U.S., with proceeds to be used to finance U.S. electricity network asset investments, including transmission and renewable energy facilities.
The offering marks a return for Iberdrola to the U.S. debt market, as the company’s first direct issuance in the U.S. since 2009. Iberdrola said that its decision to re-enter the U.S. market opens a new financing channel for the company, allowing it to expand and diversify its sources of financing.
Iberdrola is one of the largest corporate issuers of green bonds, using the instruments to fund projects including renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean transportation and waste management. The company announced plans in 2021 for its financing structure to have an increasingly higher percentage of green and sustainable products. In 2025, 99% of the financing signed by the company was sustainable, with the group’s sustainable financing as of the end of 2025 exceeding €66 billion.
The new issuance included two $800 million tranches, including a 3-year bond maturing in November 2029 with a 5.40% coupon, and a 7-year bond with a 5.85% coupon. Iberdrola said that the final cost was comparable to what it could have obtained in the Euromarket.
The offering was more than 3x oversubscribed, drawing an order book of more than $5 billion, with Iberdrola attributing strong demand to the green nature of the bonds.
Proceeds from the issuance will be used to finance or refinance electricity network assets, mainly transmission and renewable facilities in the U.S. where Iberdrola said it expects annual investments of $5 billion in the coming years.

articles.title: Radisson Hotel Group Introduces Africa’s First Verified Net Zero Hotel in South Africa - Hospitality & Catering News
articles.summary: Radisson Hotel Group Introduces Africa’s First Verified Net Zero Hotel in South Africa  Hospitality & Catering News
articles.full_text:
Radisson Hotel Group has introduced Africa’s first Verified Net Zero hotel at Radisson Safari Hotel Hoedspruit in South Africa, marking a significant milestone in the group’s international sustainability programme.
Located in Limpopo province, close to Kruger National Park and Blyde River Canyon, the 138-room hotel has undergone operational changes designed to substantially reduce its environmental impact through renewable energy, electrification, waste management, water conservation and responsible procurement.
The property is the first hotel in Africa to achieve recognition under Radisson Hotel Group’s Verified Net Zero programme, which addresses emissions across hotel operations and supply chains through a combination of carbon reduction measures and carbon removal credits.
The programme focuses on virtually eliminating Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions through electrification and renewable electricity, while reducing Scope 3 emissions associated with food and beverage, laundry, waste, amenities and procurement.
Compliance with the Net Zero Methodology for Hotels is independently verified by TÜV Rheinland.
Tim Cordon, Chief Operating Officer, Middle East, Africa and South East Asia Pacific at Radisson Hotel Group, said: “Bringing our Verified Net Zero program to Africa is an important step in making lower-carbon hospitality a practical choice across more destinations. At Hoedspruit, the natural surroundings are a defining part of why guests visit, making this a particularly meaningful place to introduce the program.
“The hotel demonstrates how investment in renewable electricity, electrification and everyday operational changes can reduce environmental impact while maintaining a compelling guest experience. It also gives our owners and teams across Africa a practical example of how existing hotels can contribute to the transition toward net zero.”
The hotel combines on-site solar generation with renewable electricity purchased through renewable energy certificates, while a solar wheeling agreement is scheduled to take effect in 2027.
Under the proposed arrangement, a renewable energy supplier will feed solar-generated electricity into South Africa’s national grid, with an equivalent contracted volume allocated to the hotel’s electricity consumption.
Electrification has also been introduced across key operational areas, including extensive use of electric kitchen equipment and heat pumps to provide hot water for guestrooms.
Electric golf carts and three-wheeled utility vehicles are being used to support daily hotel operations, reducing reliance on fossil-fuel-powered transportation within the property.
Water conservation forms another part of the hotel’s environmental programme, with Radisson reporting that 100% of the property’s wastewater is recycled through its own treatment plant.
The hotel has also introduced waste separation and recycling partnerships with local organisations.
Shodulla Recycling handles materials including plastic, glass and paper, while Egg Brothers processes food waste through composting and worm-farming initiatives.
Additional measures include bulk bathroom amenities designed to reduce single-use plastic consumption, with containers returned to suppliers through a closed-loop recycling system.
Glass water bottles and the provision of selected amenities on request are also intended to reduce unnecessary packaging and waste.
Guests are encouraged to participate in resource conservation through towel reuse and flexible housekeeping arrangements, helping reduce water consumption, energy use and cleaning products.
A digital guest information platform, STAY e-concierge, is also being introduced to reduce printed materials and improve communication between guests and hotel teams.
Food and beverage operations form an important part of the hotel’s wider sustainability strategy.
Working with food sustainability platform Klimato, Radisson Safari Hotel Hoedspruit is introducing carbon-labelled menus, providing diners with information about the estimated emissions associated with individual dishes.
The data will also help the culinary team assess ingredients, review recipes and develop lower-carbon menu options.
The approach extends to responsible procurement and supplier partnerships, including an initiative with Zanetti Collection that sees used Hausbrandt coffee bags repurposed into shopping bags by a local community sewing project.
Compostable coffee capsules and Ronnefeldt tea products incorporating recyclable packaging and compostable tea bags are among further measures intended to reduce waste.
Staff training, energy monitoring and preventative maintenance are also being incorporated into daily operations across housekeeping, engineering, front office and food and beverage departments.
Inge Huijbrechts, Chief Sustainability & Security Officer at Radisson Hotel Group, said: “Verified Net Zero requires us to look beyond a hotel’s energy supply and address the wider footprint of its operations. Independent verification by TÜV Rheinland provides a consistent framework and gives guests, owners and corporate customers greater confidence in the hotel’s credentials.
“Bringing the program to Africa is an exciting proof that Verified Net Zero can work everywhere and strengthens our understanding of how to apply this approach across different destinations as we work toward 100 Verified Net Zero hotels by 2030.”
Under the programme, residual emissions that cannot currently be eliminated are addressed through carbon removal credits.
At Hoedspruit, these credits are procured through Greentrade from the South African GRASS project, which supports grassland restoration and regenerative land management.
The approach prioritises direct emissions reductions before addressing remaining emissions through the carbon removal programme.
With views towards the Drakensberg Mountains, the hotel offers 138 rooms and suites, including accommodation with private pools, alongside restaurants, spa facilities and meeting and event spaces.
The property’s location provides access to South Africa’s wildlife and natural landscapes, with the sustainability measures incorporated into both leisure stays and business gatherings.
Radisson Safari Hotel Hoedspruit becomes the tenth hotel in the group’s Verified Net Zero portfolio, following earlier developments across the UK and Nordic markets.
The milestone supports Radisson Hotel Group’s ambition to reach 100 Verified Net Zero hotels by 2030, demonstrating how existing hospitality properties can adopt operational changes intended to reduce their environmental footprint.

articles.title: Circular economy: Africa regenerates its resources - Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.summary: Circular economy: Africa regenerates its resources  Il Sole 24 ORE
articles.full_text:
Circular economy: Africa regenerates its resources
From Kenya to South Africa: national and international initiatives for sustainable innovation
from our correspondent Alberto Magnani
ai preferiti su Google
NAIROBI - The start-up Octavia Carbon specialises in ‘capturing’ carbon dioxide. M-Taka develops waste management solutions. Mr. Green Africa collects, processes and resells plastic. All three companies were founded in Kenya between 2014 and 2022. All three are part of the ever-expanding African circular economy sector. According to figures released by the African Development Bank, the sustainable ‘transformation’ of the continent’s economy could unlock market opportunities worth around 546 billion US dollars and create 11 million jobs by 2030.
The Action Plan to 2034
The African Union, the organisation bringing together the continent’s 55 countries, is seeking to support this development with the launch in 2025 of the Continental Circular Economy Action Plan for the African Union (CEAP), an action plan developed in collaboration with the European Union to shape the transition to a circular economy over the decade from 2024 to 2034.
The CEAP forms part of Agenda 2063, the AU’s economic renewal agenda, which comprises a total of five pillar objectives: to promote ‘sustainable practices’ in sectors ranging from agriculture to industry; to strengthen waste management through local infrastructure and technologies; to create ‘millions of green jobs’, fostering regional cooperation and building ‘climate resilience’ to mitigate the effects of global warming on the continent that is most vulnerable and least equipped to cope with its consequences. This shift in economic focus goes hand in hand with two intertwined objectives on the agenda of governments both south and north of the Sahara: the optimisation of their own resources and the development of industrialisation, which is still lagging behind in the continent’s more than 50 countries, now linked within the unified framework of the African Continental Free Trade Area, set to launch in 2021.
Beyond the scope of the EAC, the continent is dotted with initiatives ranging from the South Africa Plastics Pact, launched in Pretoria in 2020, to transnational projects such as the roadmap drawn up by the African Development Bank, and regional legislative measures. One such example is the bill to harmonise the management of single-use plastics across the eight countries of the East African Community (EAC), known as the Prohibition of the Manufacture, Importation, Use and Sale of Single-Use Plastics Bill, or simply the EAC SUP Bill. The potential is as vast as it is untapped. According to an analysis by Invest Kenya, the Africa Legal Network (ALN) Kenya and TakaTaka Ni Mali, the waste sector in Kenya alone could generate up to $700 million by 2030.
“The bulk of it,” explains Ben Dixon of the consultancy firm Systemiq, “comes from transforming waste materials into resources for local industry, creating jobs and reducing dependence on imported raw materials.” Kenyan entrepreneurs, says Dixon, “are already leading this effort; the challenge now is to help them scale up”. The fundamental issue, “is not whether Africa has raw materials, a market or political ambition”, says Carlotta Dal Lago of Aln Kenya, the alliance of African law firms that drafted the “Sup Bill”. What is needed, she says, is a ‘regulatory framework’ that offers certainty to investors.

articles.title: Waste Recycling Technologies: Why Are BRICS Countries Moving Towards Circular Economy? - African Times
articles.summary: Waste Recycling Technologies: Why Are BRICS Countries Moving Towards Circular Economy?  African Times
articles.full_text:
BRICS countries are actively discussing the transition to a circular economy. Why is this needed? Which national programmes and joint initiatives are already in place? And what still needs to be done? Read the TV BRICS report
Benefits of a circular economy
A circular economy helps conserve resources, reduce the amount of waste and lower the costs of maintaining waste disposal sites. This system replaces the linear “production – use – disposal” model with a regenerative cycle and enables the global economy to reduce spending on virgin raw materials, saving tens of trillions of roubles.
Recognising this, BRICS member states are actively discussing the transition to a circular economy (CE). In September 2026, waste recycling technologies once again became an important topic of discussion at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
In addition, the circular economy is one of the main ways to achieve the eleventh Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 11) adopted by the UN. Its official name is “Ensuring the openness, safety, resilience and environmental sustainability of cities and human settlements”. At the same time, experts stress that achieving this goal requires not only financial investment but also cooperation and coordination between different types of stakeholders, both within individual countries and between groups of countries.
“The BRICS group is implementing both national programmes and joint initiatives as part of the transition to a circular economy. Despite differences in approaches, there are also common trends: a focus on developing infrastructure, encouraging waste recycling and exchanging innovative technologies,” Ekaterina Reshneva, Associate Professor at the Department of Sectoral Economics of Empress Catherine II Saint Petersburg Mining University and Candidate of Economic Sciences, said in an interview with TV BRICS.
National and joint BRICS initiatives
BRICS countries currently account for 49.5 per cent of the world’s population and around 40 per cent of global GDP. The grouping includes the world’s largest energy producers and consumers, as well as states with significant potential in critical resources and technologies. Experts consider all this an important advantage in achieving sustainable development goals.
Moreover, according to Gabriela de Fatima Cia, an expert in sustainable development, international environmental cooperation, water resources management and forest ecosystems, member of the BRICS Student Commission and coordinator of the Youth Secretariat of the Centre for Integration and Cooperation of Russia and Latin America (CICRAL), the transition to a circular economy in the BRICS founding countries is now more than realistic. However, it is highly uneven.
“The transition to a circular economy is progressing faster where infrastructure investment and compliance with legislation go hand in hand, and it stalls where legislation outpaces financing and institutional capacity,” Gabriela de Fatima Ciasays.
In this respect, China is currently the most advanced in terms of infrastructure. In 2020, a provision was added to the country’s legislation on solid waste management making household waste sorting mandatory. In addition, China completely banned the import of waste.
The country has created the world’s largest network of waste-to-energy facilities – more than 2,170 waste incineration plants processing 1.11 million tonnes per day. The “Waste-Free City” programme currently covers 113 cities, while the new national action plan for 2026–2030 sets a target of processing 45 billion tonnes of bulk waste annually.
“The National Development and Reform Commission of China (NDRC) announced the publication of a plan for developing the circular economy in the country during the implementation of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030). According to the document, by 2030, the circular economy system covering production, consumption, recycling and the reuse of resources will be further optimised,” Ekaterina Reshneva said in an interview with TV BRICS.
Brazil presents the opposite picture: strict legislation but relatively weak implementation. Since 2010, the National Solid Waste Policy has established a clear waste management hierarchy and a unique Brazilian “reverse logistics” model based on shared producer responsibility. However, in 2022, only 1.8 per cent of municipal waste was actually recycled, says Brazilian expert Gabriela de Fatima Cia. There are positive developments here as well. For example, the recycling rate for aluminium cans has reached 100 per cent.
Experts point to Brazil’s achievements in implementing technologies for composting organic waste, which can reduce the volume of such waste in landfills by 25 per cent.
Brazil is also actively using anaerobic digestion methods. As a result, two useful products are obtained: biogas, a mixture of methane and carbon dioxide, which is used to generate electricity and heat, and digestate – a high-quality organic fertiliser. Among other promising projects, experts highlight technologies for treating wastewater using fungi.
“Scientists from the Federal University of Alagoas (UFAL) in Brazil are developing a technology for treating wastewater using specially selected strains of fungi. This work is being carried out as part of a joint project with Tambov State Technical University and China Three Gorges University,” Ekaterina Reshneva says.
In Russia, the so-called waste reform began in 2019, when the collection and disposal of municipal solid waste became the responsibility of regional operators rather than municipal institutions. The goals of the reform are to combat illegal dumping and increase waste recycling. Targets were even set for recycling 60 per cent of waste. However, by 2024, around 90 per cent of waste was still being sent to landfills, and by 2020, separate waste collection had been established in only a few Russian regions, Gabriela de Fatima Cia notes.
Since 2025, Russia has been implementing the national project “Environmental Well-being”, which includes the federal project “Circular Economy”. Its targets include:
- establishing a circular economy that will ensure the sorting of 100 per cent of the volume of municipal solid waste generated annually by 2030;
- landfilling no more than 50 per cent of such waste and bringing at least 25 per cent of production and consumption waste into economic circulation as secondary resources and raw materials;
- recycling and neutralising at least 50 per cent of the total volume of Class I–II hazardous waste by 2036.
The necessary infrastructure is being developed to achieve these targets: more than 200 waste recycling plants, separate waste collection systems and facilities for processing secondary resources. As for businesses, an updated extended producer responsibility (EPR) system has been in operation in Russia since 2024, encouraging companies to develop recycling capacity and produce more environmentally friendly packaging.
India’s key government initiative for waste collection and recycling is the Clean India Mission, the second phase of which runs until the end of 2026. Over the past five years, experts say, the volume of waste sent for recycling under the programme has increased by 20 per cent. However, according to Gabriela de Fatima Cia, part of the visible progress is driven by India’s informal waste-picking economy, where millions of people earn a living by collecting and manually sorting waste, filling gaps in the government waste management system. These informal waste pickers process 15–20 per cent of all waste, including 95 per cent of the country’s electronic waste, one of the largest volumes in the world.
This informal structure is complemented by a growing municipal network. In recent years, new plants have appeared in the country, including facilities using technologies to recycle electronic waste and recover precious metals.
India’s leading co-operative recycling structure is the Material Recycling Association of India (MRAI). The association brings together national trade and recycling communities that are stakeholders in the recycling of metals, electronic waste, municipal solid waste, plastics, rubber and rubber waste, paper, glass and construction materials.
Joint BRICS initiatives in the circular economy
The transition to a circular economy and the efficient use of resources are among the key priorities on the agenda of all BRICS countries. Their joint activities are aimed at creating closed-loop supply chains, reducing waste and introducing digital recycling technologies. Experts highlight the following among the most significant projects:
- the BRICS Economic Information Exchange Platform;
- the activities of the New Development Bank;
- the BEST (BRICS Environmentally Sound Technology Platform);
- the BRICS Clean Rivers Programme;
- BRICS bioeconomy corridors;
- the BRICS STI Framework Programme.
Through the BRICS Economic Information Exchange Platform, member states can share data and expertise in the field of the circular economy. This helps identify successful cases and gaps in national strategies.
The New Development Bank actively provides funding for climate and environmental projects in renewable energy, water resource management, green infrastructure, adaptation and land restoration.

32 Lenders Back AirTrunk’s A$4.25 Billion Green Loan for SYD3 Data Centre Campus
- Green loan secured: AirTrunk has secured a A$4.25 billion green loan, backed by 32 local and international lenders, to fund its SYD3 campus in Western Sydney.
- Margin savings pledged: Any contributions from margin savings will go to AirTrunk’s social impact program for local charities.
- Completion by 2028: Construction, led by A W Edwards, is underway, with completion expected by mid-2028.
AirTrunk has secured a A$4.25 billion green loan to fund continued development of its SYD3 campus in Western Sydney. The hyperscale data centre specialist operates across Asia Pacific and the Middle East (APME). SYD3 will add capacity for cloud, artificial intelligence (AI) and enterprise services. AirTrunk expects the project to support more than 10,000 jobs across construction, trades, engineering, logistics and safety.
The facility is a green loan with margin adjustments, so its interest margin can change. Any contributions from margin savings will go to AirTrunk’s social impact program for local charities. These charities work in STEM education, digital equity, biodiversity and conservation, sustainable innovation and disaster relief. AirTrunk did not disclose the loan’s tenor, pricing or SYD3’s planned capacity.
Construction of the expanded campus, led by A W Edwards, is underway and due for completion by mid-2028. AirTrunk is using lower carbon steel and concrete on site. It also targets diverting at least 90 per cent of non-hazardous construction waste from landfill.
To support just-in-time deliveries, AirTrunk uses a 25,000 sqm buffer zone in Western Sydney to store, stage and pre-commission equipment. It has also invested in dedicated time-charter vessels serving Port Botany and Port Kembla. “SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia’s digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks. As the campus develops, it’s building a regional ecosystem through active hiring, sustained project activity and strategic supply chain partnerships – creating opportunities for local workers, contractors and businesses while delivering infrastructure Australians increasingly rely on. The green financing also reflects our view that sustainability should be built into how digital infrastructure is funded and delivered. We’re focused on responsible growth that creates lasting value for communities in the regions where we operate,” said Tom Mackellar, Vice President, Origination & Market Expansion at AirTrunk.
A consortium of 32 local and international financial institutions backed the loan. According to AirTrunk, it is one of the largest lending groups assembled for a data centre financing in Australia. Fourteen lead banks underwrote it, including National Australia Bank, MUFG Bank, BNP Paribas and Deutsche Bank. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, HSBC and United Overseas Bank acted as Green Loan Coordinators.
Australian Platform and Financing
In FY26, AirTrunk worked with 1,436 supplier entities across APAC, including 615 in Australia worth A$3.4 billion in activity. Its Australian platform spans five campuses with more than 1.2GW of capacity. The company has invested over A$12 billion in Australia and plans a further A$75 billion over the next decade. This deal lifts its total committed debt financing to about A$38.4 billion globally, including more than A$19.8 billion in Australia.

Why It Matters
The loan gives AirTrunk funded construction of new cloud and AI capacity at SYD3 through mid-2028. It also backs the company’s Net Zero 2030 target for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. With 32 lenders committed, AirTrunk could tap the same group for its planned A$75 billion Australian pipeline, if SYD3 is delivered on schedule.

Vertice Embeds EcoVadis ESG Ratings in AI Procurement Workflows
- First orchestration partner: Vertice becomes EcoVadis’ first AI procurement orchestration partner.
- ESG beside price: EcoVadis ESG ratings and scores will sit alongside Vertice data on pricing, peer benchmarks, contract terms and risk.
- Capita on board: Capita, a shared customer, already uses Vertice for procurement and EcoVadis for supplier ratings.
EcoVadis, a sustainability ratings provider, has partnered with Vertice, making the AI procurement platform its first AI procurement orchestration partner. Under the partnership, EcoVadis ESG ratings and scores will be available throughout Vertice’s procurement workflows. Procurement teams can then weigh supplier ESG performance alongside Vertice’s data on pricing, peer benchmarks, contract terms and risk.
The ERM Sustainability Institute’s latest Rate the Raters survey assessed 14 ESG ratings providers. EcoVadis ranked in the top three for both quality and usefulness among corporates and investors. “A resilient supply chain relies on sustainable procurement. By embedding trusted, verified sustainability data directly into the purchasing workflow, our partnership with Vertice ensures ESG impact is evaluated right alongside price and commercial terms – every time a decision is made,” said Annette Gevaert, SVP Alliances & Partnerships at EcoVadis.

Vertice says its procurement intelligence dataset is the largest of its kind. It covers more than 250,000 negotiated contracts and over $75 billion in global indirect spend. It also holds more than 2 million price points across more than 32,000 software-as-a-service (SaaS) vendors. “Our customers want to be able to consistently make the best purchasing decisions, through an AI-native platform and based on a single view of the most comprehensive intelligence. Partnering with EcoVadis helps us to do that. Our agentic AI orchestration platform can now deliver robust and extensive ESG data alongside our own data on price, commercial terms and wider risk factors to hit both ESG objectives and cost savings goals. Customers will receive a more comprehensive view of their vendors, meaning smarter, more rounded purchasing decisions every time,” said Roy Tuvey, CEO and Founder of Vertice.
Shared Customer and Analyst Recognition
The partnership already has shared customers, including Capita. Capita is an LSE-listed international business process outsourcing and professional services company. The companies did not disclose financial terms, pricing or a date for general availability. “Vertice powers AI procurement orchestration at Capita, and EcoVadis provides trusted sustainability ratings for our suppliers. Together, the integration of EcoVadis ratings within Vertice’s AI procurement platform embeds supplier ESG performance into every procurement decision, ensuring sustainability considerations are evaluated alongside cost, risk and commercial factors,” said Suraj Naik, Group Procurement Director and Chief Procurement Officer at Capita.
RELATED ARTICLE: EcoVadis, CO2 AI Target Scope 3 Data Gaps
This year, IDC named Vertice a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide AI-Enabled Spend Orchestration 2026. Forrester called it a Notable Vendor in a 2026 Supplier Value Management report, and Lionfish ranked it the Leader in Intake-to-Procure. G2, the B2B software review site, placed Vertice first in Procurement Orchestration in its Summer and Fall 2026 Grid Reports. “Sustainability commitments are won or lost in everyday purchasing decisions. In our 2026 IDC MarketScape, Vertice was recognized as a Leader for grounding its AI in real-world outcomes, not just process. Bringing EcoVadis’ verified ratings on more than 175,000 companies into that same workflow extends these outcomes to ESG, giving procurement teams a far more complete view of every supplier they buy from,” said Patrick Reymann, Research Director – Procurement Applications and Agents at IDC.
Why It Matters
For EcoVadis, the deal puts its ratings on more than 175,000 companies inside the tool where buyers make purchasing decisions. For Vertice, the deal lets its platform serve customers’ ESG objectives as well as their cost savings goals. If shared customers like Capita adopt it widely, the integration could become a sales route for EcoVadis ratings into Vertice’s enterprise accounts.

articles.full_text:
Masdar Raises $600 Million in Debut Blue Bond, Targeting Offshore Wind
- Debut blue bond: Masdar raised $600 million through its first blue bond for maritime renewables.
- Strong demand: The orderbook peaked at $1.5 billion, and the five-year offering was 2.5 times oversubscribed.
- Programme total: The deal lifts Masdar’s bond programme to $3.35 billion raised since 2023.
Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company (Masdar) has raised $600 million through its first blue bond, debt tied to ocean and water projects. Proceeds are earmarked for maritime renewable energy projects, including offshore wind. The five-year bond is rated AA- by S&P and Fitch. Masdar said that makes it the highest-rated public corporate blue bond globally to date.
Masdar issued the bond under its US$6 billion Global Medium Term Note Programme, used for repeat bond sales. The bond pays a 5.875% US dollar coupon and is listed on the London Stock Exchange’s International Securities Market. It was swapped into euros at a yield of 4.374%. That aligns the funding with Masdar’s European investment exposure.
Regional and international investors pushed the orderbook to a peak of $1.5 billion, according to Masdar. Seven banks acted as joint lead managers and bookrunners. They were Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole CIB, First Abu Dhabi Bank, HSBC, J.P. Morgan and Société Générale CIB. However, Masdar did not name the investors or the projects that will receive the proceeds.
Last month, Masdar updated its Green Finance Framework to include eligible blue projects such as offshore wind. Those projects must support sustainable use of oceans and water. They must also pass full impact assessments to minimise harm to biodiversity. “Our first blue bond issuance under our updated Green Finance Framework provides yet more opportunities for investors to join us in building the clean energy system of the future,” said Mazin Khan, Chief Financial Officer at Masdar. “This benchmark offering will ensure capital can be delivered where it will have the most impact, supporting the development of a more resilient blue and green economy,” Khan added.
What’s New in Masdar’s Bond Programme
The raise is Masdar’s fourth bond offering and lifts the programme total from $2.75 billion to $3.35 billion. By the end of 2025, Masdar had allocated $2.3 billion to 30 projects in 10 countries with more than 16GW of gross capacity. The updated framework aligns with blue finance guidance from the International Capital Market Association and the International Finance Corporation. Moody’s also gave it an SQS1 (Excellent) rating, its highest Sustainability Quality Score.

Why It Matters
For Masdar, the bond adds euro-matched capital reserved for maritime projects. The company’s renewable energy portfolio already exceeds 65GW, and it is targeting 100GW of energy capacity by 2030. That positions Masdar to fund new offshore wind capacity toward the 100GW goal, provided projects clear the required impact assessments.

articles.full_text:
Google Says Ignite Energy Access Partnership Enabled Over 160,000 tCO2e in Cuts in H1 2026
- Emissions estimate: Google says the partnership enabled over 160,000 tonnes of CO2 equivalent in reductions in the first half of 2026.
- Logistics tools: Google built household mapping, rural routing and supply chain models for Ignite.
- Clean cooking next: The partners are modeling community micro-grids for electric cookstoves.
Google estimates its partnership with Ignite Energy Access enabled over 160,000 tCO2e in emissions reductions in the first half of 2026. The figure, in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, is driven by 3.7 million solar devices delivered across sub-Saharan Africa since 2023. Ignite, an off-grid clean energy company, aims to connect 100 million people across Africa to electricity by 2030.
The collaboration ran for three years through Google’s Startups for Sustainable Development program, with more than 100 advisory sessions. Google said over 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa live without electricity, many relying on kerosene and candles. “The moment reliable energy reaches a community, something shifts — businesses open, children study after dark, farmers can process crops instead of watching them spoil,” said Yariv Cohen, Co-Founder and CEO of Ignite Energy Access.
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
Mapping, Routing and Satellite Tools
To locate homes missing from standard maps, the joint team combined satellite imagery and Google’s Open Buildings dataset with routing algorithms. Google researchers are also building geospatial models that add rural paths to routing constraints. Separately, Google’s Operations Research (OR) models are helping optimize Ignite’s supply chain by choosing sites for central warehouses and local mini-hubs. They balance transport costs, delivery routes, vehicle capacities and inventory expenses.
Google is also developing computer vision models with Gemini for Science to map micro-solar systems from orbit. A single rooftop panel shows up as barely one pixel in standard satellite imagery. As a result, Ignite supplies ground-truth drone imagery to fine-tune the models. The team is testing thousands of code variations to improve detection precision and recall.
RELATED ARTICLE: Google Backs Texas Electric Freight Route
Next Phase: Clean Cooking
Google and Ignite are now modeling community-level micro-grids to power electric cooking. Electric cookstoves need far more power than an individual rooftop solar kit can generate. Google did not disclose its emissions methodology, the value of its support, or a timeline for the micro-grid work.
Why It Matters
For Ignite, the partnership adds mapping, routing and warehouse planning tools to its last-mile solar delivery network. For Google, the emissions estimate counts toward its aspiration to help partners cut one gigaton of carbon-equivalent emissions annually by 2030. If the micro-grid modeling proves workable, Ignite could sell higher-demand electric cooking power to communities its solar kits already reach.
